newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Australia pips Canada, despite election.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Australia pips Canada, despite election.

text.p: International investors should continue to favour Australian and U.S. bonds over Canada, despite a welcome outcome for markets in Monday's Canadian election, analysts said on Tuesday.
"In the short-term, there will be relief for the Canadian markets from the result," said David Bloom, international economist at HSBC James Capel in London.
"But we are still favouring switching out of Canada and into Australia -- economies take a long time to turn in the cycle."
The ruling Liberals retained power in Canada.
The governing party's majority was greatly reduced, but analysts said the result reassured markets, which had feared a minority government.
"The Canadian dollar and the bond market were starting to build in a minority result," said Michael Derks, cross market fixed income strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.

The Canadian dollar was trading at 1.3736/41 U.S. dollars at 1040 GMT, after rallying on the results. The 10-year Canada/U.S. spread pushed further into negative territory, with Canadian yields 20 basis points below T-notes.
"In the short-term I am very positive," said Bloom, adding that the Liberals had already proved their budget-balancing credentials in the last parliament.
But continued support for the separatist Bloc Quebecois could rattle international investors, Bloom said.

The Bloc Quebecois lost its role as official opposition to the Western Canada-based right-wing Reform Party, but still won 44 of Quebec's 75 seats. Reform had a strong showing in Western Canada, while the Liberals monopolised Ontario.
"We have Bloc Quebecois, Block West and Block Ontario -- the voting has become more factional and more regional, and that could be problematic in the medium term," said Bloom.
Canada like the U.S. was more likely to raise rates, while interest rates are moving in the other direction in Australia, analysts said.
One analyst at Credit Lyonnais in London forecast 10-year Canadian bond yields flat with U.S. Treasuries on a three-month horizon.
"The market is quite vulnerable, with an interest rate hike from the Bank of Canada likely now the election is out of the way."
Other analysts thought Canada would hold fire on raising rates until there was further tightening from the U.S. Federal Reserve.
But Canadian bonds were no match for the bullish Australian bond market, they said, which was benefiting from the surprise half point cut in interest rates to 5.5 percent on May 23.
Long-dated Australian bond yields struck their lowest level since mid-February on Tuesday, and several non-government borrowers issued bonds.
The 10-year Australia/U.S. spread was quoted at 73 basis points at 1112 GMT.
"The spread came in from 130 to 66 basis points in a very short time," said Derks. "It could go down to 50 basis points over the next month or two, and further out even to 25 basis points."
European investors were also likely to plump for U.S. Treasuries in preference to Canadian bonds, the Credit Lyonnais analyst said.
"U.S. Treasuries are a more natural safe haven for European investors concerned about EMU (European economic and monetary union) than Canadian bonds."
